sections.text: match compares a value against patterns and runs the code for the first one that fits. It's like a supercharged if/else.

A match must cover every possible case. If you add a variant and forget it somewhere, the program won't compile. Use _ to mean "anything else", but a _ arm also catches any variant you add later, so the compiler can't warn you about it.
Patterns can pull data out of variants, and match works on numbers and ranges too:

Two new tricks there. Some(x) if x < 0 is a match guard: the arm only fits when the extra if condition is true as well. 1..=9 is a range pattern: it fits any number from 1 to 9, including both ends. Arms are tried from top to bottom, so 250 skips the first three and lands on Some(x).
When you only care about one pattern, if let is shorter:
format! works like println! but gives you back a String instead of printing it.
Exhaustiveness checking is what makes enums safe to refactor. Rust also has let-else: let Some(x) = opt else { return; }; for early exits.

In the exercise, advice returns &'static str. That's a string slice that stays valid for the whole program, which is true of every string literal like "Wear sunscreen". The 'static part is called a lifetime; Unit 7 explains lifetimes.

exercise.prompt:
